div.p: BACKGROUND Extracranial metastasis from meningiomas is rare, with pulmonary involvement being the most frequent metastatic site. The authors present this case to highlight the diagnostic and management challenges associated with atypical meningiomas that metastasize outside the CNS, and to emphasize the importance of long-term surveillance even in patients with radiologically stable disease.

OBSERVATIONS A 33-year-old male was initially diagnosed with an intracranial atypical meningioma (WHO grade II, 2007 classification) characterized by increased cellularity, mild nuclear atypia, and a mitotic index ≥ 4 mitoses per 10 high-power fields, without brain invasion. Seven years later, he developed multiple pulmonary metastases confirmed by histopathological analysis. Given the absence of symptoms and minimal progression of pulmonary lesions over a 7-year follow-up period, the patient was managed conservatively with structured surveillance, including regular cranial MRI and chest CT imaging.

LESSONS This case demonstrates that long-term stability of pulmonary metastases from atypical meningioma is possible under conservative management. Structured surveillance with periodic cranial and thoracic imaging may be appropriate for asymptomatic patients, while reserving surgical or radiotherapy options for those with progressive or symptomatic disease.

Meningiomas are tumors that arise from meningothelial cells of the arachnoid mater, accounting for approximately 30% of all intracranial tumors in adults. 1 Typically, these tumors are solitary, slow-growing lesions associated with favorable prognoses. However, a subset demonstrates atypical or malignant behavior characterized by aggressive growth patterns, recurrence, and rare extracranial metastases. 2,3 Extracranial metastatic meningiomas represent an exceedingly rare clinical phenomenon, occurring in < 1% of all meningioma cases. Among extracranial metastases, pulmonary involvement is most frequently reported; however, other sites, including bones, the liver, and lymph nodes, may also be involved. The precise mechanisms underlying extracranial metastases remain poorly understood, contributing to diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. 4,5 This report presents a unique case of atypical meningioma with multiple pulmonary metastases. The rationale for documenting this case is to highlight the diagnostic and management challenges of extracranial meningioma metastases, to emphasize the role of structured long-term surveillance, and to contribute to the limited literature regarding conservative management strategies for asymptomatic pulmonary lesions. [3][4][5][6]

div.head: Illustrative Case
div.p: A 33-year-old male presented 13 years ago with progressive headaches lasting several months. The neurological examination at admission revealed mild cognitive slowing, but no focal motor or sensory deficits. MRI of the brain showed a left frontal extra-axial lesion, and he underwent craniotomy with resection of the mass. Histopathologal analysis confirmed atypical meningioma (WHO grade II) according to the 2007 WHO classification, based on increased cellularity, mild nuclear atypia, and a mitotic count of ≥ 4 mitoses per 10 high-power fields. At that time, brain invasion was not identified. While the tumor was graded according to the 2007 criteria, its features would also meet the diagnostic threshold for WHO grade 2 under the 2021 classification system. Over the following years, the patient experienced two episodes of local recurrence. The first recurrence developed approximately 4 years after the initial resection and was managed with grosstotal resection of the recurrent left frontal lesion. A second recurrence occurred about 3 years later, presenting as a new enhancing durabased mass adjacent to the prior resection site; this was again surgically removed, followed by adjuvant fractionated cranial radiotherapy

(60 Gy in 30 fractions). Subsequent follow-up imaging over the next 3-4 years demonstrated postoperative dural enhancements without evidence of progressive tumor growth. In recent follow-ups, residual intracranial lesions remained stable, with no progressive symptoms (Fig. 1). No relevant family, psychosocial, or genetic history was identified in this patient. Physical examinations conducted over the follow-up period revealed no significant abnormalities aside from mild neurological deficits related to previous surgical interventions.

Approximately 7 years after the initial diagnosis, the patient presented with gradually progressive shortness of breath and dry cough. These symptoms prompted chest imaging, as no prior thoracic studies had been performed. Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules, which were initially suspected to represent inflammatory or granulomatous disease. However, subsequent transthoracic needle aspiration biopsy confirmed metastatic meningioma, consistent histologically with the original intracranial lesion (Fig. 2). Histopathological examination of both intracranial and pulmonary lesions revealed features consistent with atypical meningioma, including increased cellularity, sheet-like growth patterns, occasional mitotic figures (≥ 4 mitoses per 10 high-power fields), and mild nuclear atypia. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated strong positivity for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) and vimentin, confirming the meningioma diagnosis and excluding other differential considerations.
No diagnostic challenges or significant adverse events were encountered during patient management.

Over a subsequent 5-year follow-up, pulmonary lesions demonstrated only minimal millimetric growth; hence, no additional therapeutic interventions were deemed necessary. Given the stable intracranial disease, asymptomatic pulmonary involvement, and multidisciplinary evaluation, the medical team opted for conservative management with routine surveillance rather than pursuing surgical or adjuvant chemotherapeutic interventions (Fig. 3).

The patient is being monitored in a multidisciplinary clinic, where neurological examinations are performed every 6 months. Additionally, cranial MRI studies are conducted every 6 months for the first 2 years and annually thereafter, and thoracic imaging (contrast-enhanced chest CT) is performed every 6-12 months. Imaging is advanced earlier if new respiratory or neurological symptoms develop. Criteria for treatment escalation include radiological progression (e.g., > 20% increase in the sum of diameters of target pulmonary nodules or the appearance of new lesions) or the development of symptoms attributable to the pulmonary disease. The intracranial disease has also remained radiologically stable during the same period, with no evidence of progression or new lesions on serial cranial MRI studies performed during the follow-up of pulmonary metastases.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Extracranial metastasis from meningiomas is exceedingly rare, occurring in < 1% of all cases. When metastatic spread occurs, the lungs are the most common site, representing approximately 60% of cases, followed by bone (approximately 26%), liver (approximately 19%), lymph nodes, and pleura. 7,8 This distribution aligns well with the clinical presentation of our patient, who exhibited pulmonary involvement, highlighting the necessity of considering metastatic potential even in atypical meningiomas.

Metastasis predominantly occurs in high-grade meningiomas, including atypical (WHO grade II) and anaplastic (WHO grade III) types. The tumor in this case was graded according to the 2007 WHO classification, which defined atypical meningioma as lesions showing ≥ 4 mitoses per 10 high-power fields, brain invasion, or at least three of five histological features, including increased cellularity, small cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, prominent nucleoli, sheet-like architecture, and spontaneous necrosis. 7,8 Our patient's tumor met the mitotic and cytological criteria for grade II without brain invasion. Although molecular parameters, such as TERT promoter mutations or CDKN2A/B homozygous deletions, are now incorporated into the 2021 WHO classification, these tests were not available at the time of diagnosis. Although rare, cases of metastasis from benign (WHO grade I) meningiomas have also been documented. 9 Key risk factors for metastatic meningiomas include male sex, tumor recurrence, high mitotic rates, location away from the skull base, involvement of venous sinuses, and certain histological features indicating higher-grade malignancy. 5,10 Our patient's tumor histopathology revealed typical features of atypical meningioma, such as increased cellularity, nuclear atypia, elevated mitotic activity, and robust immunoreactivity for EMA and vimentin, consistent with previously described metastatic atypical meningiomas. The interval from initial diagnosis to the detection of extracranial metastasis typically averages between 6 and 8 years, although earlier presentation, as seen in our case, has been reported in the literature. 6,13,14 Prognosis varies significantly based on histological grade, with a median survival following detection of metastasis generally ranging from 30 to 36 months. Patients initially diagnosed with grade I meningiomas tend to have notably better outcomes, whereas those with higher-grade tumors (grades II and III) exhibit more aggressive clinical courses and reduced survival. 15,16 Therapeutically, management of metastatic meningiomas remains challenging due to their rarity and clinical heterogeneity. Resection is generally considered the first-line approach, especially for symptomatic lesions or those causing functional impairment. Radiotherapy and chemotherapy have shown limited efficacy, and their roles remain poorly defined. 17 For asymptomatic cases with minimal lesion progression, as in our patient, conservative management involving regular imaging surveillance remains a rational and widely adopted strategy. Although both radiotherapy and systemic chemotherapy were considered in the management of our patient, neither was initiated. The rationale was based on the radiological stability of the pulmonary lesions over a 5-year period and the absence of symptoms. Current reports indicate that radiotherapy is typically reserved for progressive or symptomatic extracranial metastases, whereas conservative surveillance remains acceptable for stable disease. [18][19][20] In light of the patient's prolonged radiological stability and absence of symptoms, we adopted a structured surveillance strategy: cranial MRI and chest CT at 6-month intervals during the first 2 years, followed by annual assessments, with earlier reassessment if symptoms emerge. This pragmatic schedule aims to detect clinically meaningful progression promptly while avoiding overtreatment in indolent, asymptomatic pulmonary metastases.

Clinicians should maintain a high degree of suspicion for extracranial metastasis in patients with recurrent or atypical meningiomas. Regular surveillance imaging, including periodic thoracic and abdominal scans, is recommended to facilitate early detection and intervention. 4,21 Advances in understanding molecular markers such as TERT promoter mutations, CDKN2A/B alterations, and other genetic factors may enhance prognostic assessment and guide potential targeted therapeutic strategies in the future. [22][23][24] Although DOTATATE PET/CT imaging was not performed in this patient, it may offer additional diagnostic and surveillance benefits in FIG. 3. Follow-up MR images 2 years postoperatively. A: Axial T1-weighted postcontrast image showing stable postoperative changes without residual or recurrent enhancing lesions. B: Axial FLAIR sequence demonstrating minimal persistent edema without new pathological findings. C: Coronal T1-weighted postcontrast image confirming a stable resection site, with no evidence of recurrent intracranial disease.

to identify meningioma tissue with high sensitivity and specificity, often detecting lesions not visible on conventional MRI or CT. Recent studies have suggested that DOTATATE PET can help differentiate recurrent tumors from posttreatment changes and guide radiotherapy planning or systemic peptide receptor radionuclide therapy. In patients with known or suspected extracranial metastases, it may also assist in detecting occult systemic spread. Incorporating such molecular imaging in future follow-up protocols could enhance early detection and treatment stratification for high-grade or metastatic meningiomas. [22][23][24] Limitations of this report include its single-case nature and the rarity of extracranial metastatic meningiomas, limiting generalization and the establishment of definitive management guidelines. Further research and multi-institutional collaborations are necessary to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying biology, optimal surveillance strategies, and most effective therapeutic interventions for metastatic meningiomas. Another limitation of this case is the absence of molecular genetic studies, such as neurofibromatosis type 2, TERT, or CDKN2A/B analysis, which could have provided additional prognostic insight but were unavailable for this patient.

In conclusion, extracranial metastasis from meningiomas, while rare, predominantly affects the lungs, followed by bones, liver, lymph nodes, and pleura. Recognition of this metastatic potential, particularly in recurrent or atypical meningiomas, is essential for timely diagnosis and appropriate management. Resection remains the primary therapeutic strategy for symptomatic lesions, while conservative management with regular imaging surveillance is justified for asymptomatic or minimally progressing cases. Advances in molecular and genetic profiling may offer improved prognostic insights and guide future targeted therapeutic approaches. In our patient, conservative follow-up with structured imaging surveillance has proven effective over a 5-year period, underlining the value of individualized, symptom-oriented management for metastatic atypical meningioma.

div.head: Observations
div.p: Our patient, a 33-year-old male with recurrent atypical meningioma, developed pulmonary metastases that remained radiologically stable and asymptomatic over a 5-year follow-up period. Conservative management with routine imaging surveillance was pursued rather than surgical or adjuvant interventions.

div.head: Lessons
div.p: This case demonstrates that pulmonary metastases from atypical meningioma may remain indolent for years under surveillance. For asymptomatic patients with stable disease, a structured follow-up approach with periodic cranial and thoracic imaging can be a safe and effective option, reserving invasive treatment modalities for cases with radiological progression or clinical deterioration.
